extracted.intended_audience: artisans, scribes, instrument-makers, dyers, bookbinders and physicians (Renaissance craftsmen and technicians)
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance Latin practical manual giving prescriptive rules and technical criteria for measurement, textile work, colors and stains, book production and numbering, mechanical instruments, and medicinal selection and diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mensura ratione ponderis ad purum aurum
rubrics_metrics.description: Use weight-based measurement for pure gold rather than bubble/volume methods; the pure gold should be measured by weight because bubbles (bullae) are not admissible and this reduces variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text admonishes that for pure gold the mensura (measure) is by weight (ratio ponderis); avoid methods admitting air-bubbles; heavier (weight) standards vary less and therefore give maximal perfection. Example contrast: argentum vivum weighs differently and is not as perfectly measured by bubble methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accipere mensuram maximam in unoquoque genere
rubrics_metrics.description: In every class/genre choose the greatest (most inclusive/stable) standard of measure to minimize relative error when working down to smaller subdivisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states 'A maximis autem in unoquoque genere mensuram accipere debemus; ut ad minima dis... minor error contingat.' The practical rule is to use the largest convenient unit for the type of thing you measure so that subdivision errors are minimized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtilitas et robur in texturis (fineness vs. strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fineness (subtilitas) in woven goods is desirable but must be combined with strength (robur): fine threads joined to a solid structure give better, longer-lasting fabrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: byssus and very thin threads (Bernucium) can make superior and durable textiles if coupled with robustness; fine thread alone is not always best. The text stresses that nature and art both supply qualities—use species (material) and technique to achieve both fineness and solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abluere maculas pingues (removal of greasy stains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greasy (fat) stains are removed by applying a proper detergent, compressing the treated spot between boards and linen for an extended period (about 24 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'Pingues verò maculas valde; terunt ... tenuissimo aboleri; cum super maculam inserius per horas xxiiij inter tabulas ac lintea comprimitur.' Do not attempt to wash out certain colorants that will be lost; choose detergents appropriate to the stain (soap, oil-pungent treatment) and use pressure/time to extract the stain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color recipes and mixing (cocco purpureus, brasilium, indico, glasto)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescriptions for pigments and how to combine them to obtain colors: e.g., cocco purpureus, rubens brasili for reds; indigo and glasto (weld) with violet to obtain green; atramentum (ink) for black.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists specific pigments and notes how additives change hue ('indico & glasto j[addito] violeto; fine quo locus est viridi'). It also warns that some color treatments will fade or be lost if washed; choose pigment combinations and fixatives appropriate to the desired permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicata textura: manufacture of extremely thin yet durable goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for producing very thin (tenuissima) textiles and articles that nevertheless have durability: use appropriate yarn counts, combinations, and finishing methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: very thin threads in garments and special named kinds (Bernucium). The author notes that parts fitted together in thin materials may hold better than coarse ones and that this affects cost and desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce duplicate exemplaria simultaneously (double/quadruple-thread binding)
rubrics_metrics.description: When copying or producing multiple exemplars, use doubled or quadrupled thread and joinings so that two (or more) books can be produced at once and be nearly identical in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'Inde duplici filo ... duo capies exemplaria penitus similia iuxta typi unius forma.' The practical advice is to run multiple threads through the same sewing so that two copies can be completed together; glue and connect sheets appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book assembly by gluing and short concentrated labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble and order booklets by attaching clean leaves with glue and working in a short concentrated period (three days) rather than transcribing piecemeal over a long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'Glutine aliquo sublata libellorum frutta chartis annectes puris. Ita tridui laboret totum libri melius in ordinem ac facilius rediges, quam si toto anno transcribendo labores.' Use glue to bind clean sheets and organize work to complete a book in days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular numeral system for representing large numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transverse figures and tabular placements (tabula, transversa line) to record and combine large numbers without confusion; represent magnitudes by positions and transverse marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives examples (1000,2000... and later 9000 figures) and demonstrates how to write 12509, 25553 etc by placing figures in side/transverse positions so sums and augmentations are visually unambiguous. This is a prescriptive method for storage/indexing of numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering supplements and 'prima/ secunda additio' rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding supplements to a written work, assign them to ordinal 'additions' (prima additio, secunda additio, etc.) and place their numbering in corresponding tables so reading and assembling is unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: note where each added set of folios belongs, mark its number in the appropriate tabula (first/second addition), and when reading place supplements in the indicated order to avoid confusion. If the first addition of a supplement is to be read, follow the rules about which supplement follows which in the reading sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indexed letters/boards to teach the blind to write
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach a blind person to write by using a board with letters formed (cavities) and providing a stylus that traces the letters by touch, with long practice to develop habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'Tabula mea cauis literis ordine alphabeti calatur ... stylist per singula deducit elementa, memoria tenens illo; pervicescitur.' Requires persistent practice and a fine stylus; many learn with difficulty but can do so with time and supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulley, counterweight and balance principles for ascent and descent
rubrics_metrics.description: When ascending/descending by rope, use pulley/trochlea and counterweights; set the counterweight slightly lighter than the body so you can be pulled up or lowered safely and quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed mechanical example: attach a hook and pulley, place a counterweight slightly less than the user's weight so that the user can climb or be drawn up; the text gives letters and proportions (A, B, C, D...) and warns about lateral pull due to offset weight and ways to prevent slipping by design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forcipé (clamps) and cochlea (helical device) for controlled rope work
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ clamps and a helical iron cochlea (a hollow spiral) with a perforated capsule to engage and hold rope for rapid descent/ascent in a controlled and safe manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction details: cochlea of steel the length of the palm, hollow inside to receive the rope; a light capsule above and below perforated holds pegs which engage the rope; when the rope is tightened the device advances smoothly—prevents slips and allows even an inexperienced person to rely on it safely. The text contrasts safe devices vs. unsafe improvised sticks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of beam-support lifting instrument (proportion and placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To lift or support heavy beams, arrange small pedicels and supports at appropriate distances and heights—the projecting length of the beam and the position of supports determine the ability to elevate the beam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: if the projecting part is too little the beam cannot be elevated; if too little perpendicular distance to fulcrum differs and aggravates the lift. The passage prescribes how to place supports (AB, CP etc.) so that the beam is secure and can be raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for mutual sustentation (objects supporting one another)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several pieces sustain one another, ensure proportions and contact so that the assembly is stable; when one piece is appropriately placed it can sustain others and none will fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples of beams and small supports—if each part is proportionate and placed correctly, the whole structure will be firm. The maxim: the more pressed (compacted) an object is, the firmer it is; but it must not be so tight that something else breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-of-gravity demonstration prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate demonstrations of balance and center of gravity require a perfectly flat abacus surface, a straight rod, and precise placement of the fulcrum and weights; otherwise the phenomenon fails and experimenters may be misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a careful experimental protocol: abacus surface must be true, wood straight and not too thin, and the fulcrum and points exactly placed; only then will the rod remain suspended as the geometric demonstration predicts. It warns that crude experiments will mislead the unlearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary medicinal qualities: hot, cold, moist, dry
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine and bodies are governed by four primary qualities (calidum, frigidum, humidum, siccum); these determine the action of drugs and should be matched against the patient's condition (hot to cold, cold to hot, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains operations of each quality (heat: soften, cook, melt; cold: harden, preserve, congeal; moist: loosen, make softer; dry: make harder). Secondary qualities and further operations derive from these. Practical rule: choose medicines whose qualities will balance or remove pathological qualities in the patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of the best portion of liquids and substances for remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing wine, oil, honey or similar for medicinals, prefer certain portions of the vessel: for wine the middle is best, for honey the densest (bottom) is best; avoid top or bottom if vitiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'Optimum igitur in medio ... Mellissimum probatur quod dulcedine laudé mereatur. Porró dulcissimum; quod de sum maximé densum ...' This is practical selection guidance: the middle fraction of wine is most robust; honey's best is the densest part at the bottom; oils also have preferable parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing medicines: avoid superfluous admixtures; balance efficacy and harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A good medicine is constructed so that superfluous (harmful) constituents are minimized and the useful principle is preserved—the stronger (potent) constituent should be chosen so the remedy acts strongly but not dangerously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author refers to traditional Theriac and warns against adding substances for vainglory; says experience (experientia) shows when something should be added or withheld. When joining strong substances, keep in mind the risk of harm; match the strength of the remedy to the patient's constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical subtilitas: prefer natural subtlety and fluidity in speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtlety in speech (division, accent, choice of phrasing) is powerful but must be natural and liquid; affected subtlety is displeasing and less effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes types of subtlety (grammaticus, sophista, mathematicus, physicus) and recommends that imitation of nature—clarity and flowing phrasing—wins in oratory. Artificially affected subtlety separates one from art; natural subtlety pleases most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of clouds and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds appear flat and nearer the earth from a given viewpoint due to geometric perspective; to judge their form and distance, apply geometric ratios and angles rather than assuming spherical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author sets up geometric points and ratios (A, B, C... lines and angles) to show why clouds over the head appear inclined and nearer to the observer; concludes that many clouds are planar rather than spherical based on visual proportion and distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urine-based diagnosis: sediment, clarity and heat effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In clinical diagnosis by urine, observe the position of sediment (usually at bottom), the thinness/clarity (thin urine may indicate heated or subtle states), and turbidity (fatness produces turbidity); these characteristics indicate underlying conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'Urina continet sedimentum sola; in ima tantum parte ... Urina tenuis valde subitata ob calorem ... Urina ventris influitioni prode longe magis aquae falsa.' The practical advice: use sediment, clarity, and effects of heat to infer illness (e.g., thin urine penetrates internal parts; heat makes urine clearer; turbidity may indicate excess fat/humors).
